clue.text: Narcissus, possibly?

parts.note: Narcissus is both a spring flower and the beautiful young man of Greek myth, so the clue points at a flower and at a youth in his prime

explanation.surface: A query about whether the vain figure of myth fits some description.
explanation.walkthrough: The phrase works both ways: a narcissus is literally a bloom, and the mythical Narcissus is the picture of a beautiful young man at his peak.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase means the freshness and beauty of young people, which the flower and the mythical young man both embody.

clue.text: Attention perhaps initially engaged by little enclosure in zoo?

indicators.note: to be engaged by something is to be held inside it, so the other pieces sit within the word for little

parts.note: a bit is a little amount
to give someone your ear is to pay attention

indicators.note: initially points to the opening letter of the word perhaps

explanation.surface: Wondering whether a small zoo pen first caught the public's attention.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads as a question about publicity; 'Attention' is really an ear, and the question mark admits a bear pit is only one kind of zoo enclosure.
explanation.definitionFit: A sunken pit where bears were kept for display is a classic feature of old zoos.

clue.text: Actor one's seen in a musical

indicators.note: being seen in something places one piece within another

parts.note: Oliver! is the Lionel Bart stage musical based on Oliver Twist
one is the Roman numeral I; the 's stands for 'is'

explanation.surface: A performer who appears in a stage musical.
explanation.walkthrough: 'seen in' puts I inside OLIVER, the musical adapted from Dickens.
explanation.definitionFit: Laurence Olivier was one of the most celebrated English stage and film performers of the twentieth century.

clue.text: Manoeuvre in which guy secures new deal

indicators.note: to secure something is to hold it fast, here by enclosing the other letters

parts.note: a guy is a male person
a hand is the set of cards dealt to a player, so a deal can mean a hand

explanation.surface: Describing a political move in which a man locks down a fresh agreement.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Guy' and 'new deal' suggest politics, but the deal is a hand of cards and the guy simply a male.
explanation.definitionFit: To shift something roughly by hand, often heavy or awkward, is to steer it physically into place.

clue.text: Concentrate, form of cordial, originally American

indicators.note: to form the word of anew is to rearrange its two letters
originally points to the first letter of cordial

explanation.surface: Describing a type of soft drink concentrate that began in America.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Concentrate' and 'cordial' together suggest a fruit drink, but 'Concentrate' is a verb, and 'form' works on the little word 'of'.
explanation.definitionFit: To focus is to direct all one's attention onto one thing, which is to concentrate.

clue.text: Musical piece and other things turning up in books on subtonic

indicators.note: one piece sits in another, so the reversed letters go within the books

parts.note: OT is the Old Testament, a set of books of the Bible

indicators.note: in a down clue turning up means reading the letters from bottom to top, so backwards

parts.note: etc. (et cetera) means and other things
te is the seventh note in tonic sol-fa, the note just below the tonic

explanation.surface: A composition and assorted items surfacing among volumes resting on a low note.
explanation.walkthrough: 'on' in a down clue means placed below, so the subtonic note comes last; the subtonic (te) is the seventh degree of the scale in tonic sol-fa.
explanation.definitionFit: This variant spelling names a composition written for eight players or voices.

clue.text: Translated long article inspirational passage

parts.note: TR is a standard abbreviation for translated or translator
to long for something is to ache for it
a is the indefinite article

explanation.surface: Describing a lengthy item rendered from another language, full of uplifting prose.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Inspirational passage' reads as uplifting prose but means the airway through which breath is drawn in.
explanation.definitionFit: The windpipe is the tube that carries inhaled air to the lungs, so it is literally a passage for breathing in.

clue.text: What's involved in vain attempt to make waves

definitions.text: What's involved in vain attempt to make waves

parts.words: What's involved in vain attempt to make waves
parts.note: making waves sounds like stirring trouble, but here it means growing curls, a vain bid by the balding to regain a full head

explanation.surface: Asking what goes into a futile effort to cause a stir.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Vain' means both futile and conceited, and 'waves' means both disruption and wavy hair; the product a balding person uses fits both readings.
explanation.definitionFit: A tonic or lotion sold to make lost hair grow back is the tool of anyone hoping for waves on top again.

clue.text: Article about first-class drinking establishment over in Middle East?

indicators.note: one piece placed about another goes round it

parts.note: an is the indefinite article

indicators.note: over signals that the letters are turned round

parts.note: A1 means first-class; it is written AI here
a bar is a place for drinking

explanation.surface: A guide entry on a top-rated pub abroad in the Gulf region.
explanation.walkthrough: 'over' turns AIBAR into RABIA, and 'about' puts that inside AN. A1 (first-class) is read as the letters A and I.
explanation.definitionFit: Arabia is the great peninsula of the Middle East, so belonging there makes one of that region.

clue.text: Weapon, type deployed around Utah

indicators.note: a piece deployed around another is spread round it, enclosing it

parts.note: a class is a type or category
UT is the postal abbreviation for the US state of Utah

explanation.surface: A kind of armament sent into action in a western American state.
explanation.walkthrough: US state abbreviations are common crossword fodder; here the postal code sits inside a word for a type.
explanation.definitionFit: A short curved sword with a broad blade, once favoured by sailors and pirates.

clue.text: On of the snags with fishnet stockings?

definitions.text: On of the snags with fishnet stockings

parts.words: On of the snags with fishnet stockings
parts.note: a run in hosiery is called a ladder, and fishnet points to a fish, so the clue pictures a ladder in a fish's stockings

explanation.surface: Complaining about a drawback of wearing net tights.
explanation.walkthrough: A ladder is a run in tights or stockings; 'fishnet' supplies the fish. The real thing is a series of steps letting salmon swim upstream past a weir.
explanation.definitionFit: A fish ladder is a stepped channel that lets migrating fish leap past a dam, here pictured as a run in hosiery.

clue.text: Copy article on Germany, typically heartless

indicators.note: in an across clue one piece on another follows it
heartless means the central letters are taken out of the word

parts.note: Germany is an example of a republic
a is the indefinite article

explanation.surface: Duplicate a German newspaper item, with the usual cold detachment.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Germany, typically' reads as a comment on German habits, but it names Germany as an example of a form of state.
explanation.definitionFit: A replica is an exact reproduction of an original, which is a copy.

clue.text: The class would need more than one

definitions.text: The class would need more than one

parts.words: The class would need more than one
parts.note: a whole class of pupils needs several school bags; also, the letters of the class rearrange to give the plural of the bag

explanation.surface: A remark about how many of something a school group requires.
explanation.walkthrough: Every pupil carries a school bag, so a class needs many; and THE CLASS is an anagram of the plural, a bonus the solver can spot after solving.
explanation.definitionFit: A shoulder bag for carrying school books, one per pupil.

clue.text: Persian queen leaving horse in compound

indicators.note: something leaving a word is removed from it

parts.note: Esther was the Jewish queen of the Persian king in the Old Testament
H is slang for heroin, which is also called horse

explanation.surface: A Persian royal riding away and leaving her mount in an enclosure.
explanation.walkthrough: 'leaving' removes H (heroin, slang 'horse') from ESTHER. 'Compound' looks like an enclosure for the horse but is the chemical sense.
explanation.definitionFit: An ester is a chemical compound formed when an acid reacts with an alcohol.

clue.text: Ruffian turned funny, clutching end of huge galvanised spear

indicators.note: to clutch something is to hold it, so the outer piece wraps the rest
turned signals the letters are read backwards

parts.note: funny means odd or peculiar

indicators.note: end of picks the last letter of the word huge
galvanised means jolted into action, so the letters of spear are shaken up

explanation.surface: A thug turned strange, gripping a huge zinc-coated spear.
explanation.walkthrough: 'galvanised' means stirred into action, signalling a rearrangement; 'turned' applies only to the word for funny.
explanation.definitionFit: A desperado is a reckless criminal of the Wild West kind, a ruffian ready for anything.

clue.text: Air of religiosity?

parts.note: air can mean a tune as well as a manner, and religiosity points to the soul, so the clue is a tune with a spiritual feel

explanation.surface: Describing someone's pious manner.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Air' suggests a manner or bearing, but here it is a melody; the genre grew from gospel singing in Black churches.
explanation.definitionFit: A genre of popular song rooted in gospel and rhythm and blues, with a strongly emotional, spiritual feel.

clue.text: Collection of material prior to joining service

definitions.text: Collection of material prior to joining service

parts.words: Collection of material prior to joining service
parts.note: joining service suggests enlisting, but the service is a wedding and the material is the clothes and linen a bride gathers

explanation.surface: Kit gathered by a recruit before enlisting in the forces.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Joining service' points to the armed forces, but the service is a marriage service, and the material is fabric for the bride's clothes and linen.
explanation.definitionFit: A bride's outfit of clothes and household linen, gathered in readiness for married life.

clue.text: Old, bald eccentric?

indicators.note: eccentric means off-centre or irregular, so the letters are arranged oddly

explanation.surface: Picturing a bald old man with peculiar habits.
explanation.walkthrough: 'eccentric' rearranges OLD and BALD; the whole clue also describes the answer, a strange old bald fellow.
explanation.definitionFit: An oddball is a strange or unconventional person, which an eccentric old man would be called.

clue.text: Unbeliever's endless criticism about church and priest

definitions.note: the 's stands for 'is', joining the definition to the wordplay

indicators.note: one piece about another wraps round it
endless means the final letter is cut off

parts.note: stick is informal for harsh criticism, as in giving someone stick
CE is the Church of England

explanation.surface: A doubter keeps nagging about religion and the clergy.
explanation.walkthrough: Giving someone 'stick' is British slang for harsh criticism; 'endless' trims that word before it goes round the church and priest.
explanation.definitionFit: A sceptic doubts accepted claims, especially religious ones, so is a person without belief.

clue.text: Student at university, one in Poland

indicators.note: the letters go in the abbreviation for the country

parts.note: PL is the international code for Poland
up means in residence at a university, as in up at Oxford
I is the Roman numeral one

explanation.surface: A student at a university in Poland.
explanation.walkthrough: In British usage you are 'up' at university while attending it, as in 'up at Cambridge'.
explanation.definitionFit: A pupil is someone being taught, a learner or student.

clue.text: Scientist developing debugging process

parts.note: debugging suggests fixing computer code, but here the bugs are germs and the process is the heat treatment that kills them in milk

explanation.surface: A computer scientist designing a method for fixing code errors.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Debugging' reads as software work, but the bugs are microbes; the French chemist gave his name to pasteurisation.
explanation.definitionFit: The nineteenth-century French microbiologist devised the heating method that kills harmful microbes in food.

clue.text: Enclosure designed for recent issue

parts.note: an enclosure for a recent issue sounds like a magazine supplement, but the issue is offspring, a newly arrived baby

explanation.surface: An insert made for the latest edition of a magazine.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Enclosure' and 'issue' suggest a magazine insert, but 'issue' means children, and the enclosure is where a toddler is put to play safely.
explanation.definitionFit: A small fenced pen where a baby or toddler can play safely.

clue.text: Typically, beef trade's badly affected around Middle East

indicators.note: the rearranged letters go around the other piece
something badly affected is damaged, so the letters of trade are disordered

parts.note: the 's only shows possession or stands for 'is', so it adds no letters: the word before it gives these letters as it is written

explanation.surface: The beef business suffers from events in the Middle East.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Typically' marks beef as one example of the answer; the surface suggests a trade crisis, but 'trade' is just anagram fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: Beef is the standard example of meat from cattle and other mammals that is dark when raw.

clue.text: The untimely death of Richard crowns victor of Bosworth Field

indicators.note: the crowns of words are their tops, which in a down answer means their first letters

explanation.surface: Richard III's early death on the battlefield brings the throne to the winner.
explanation.walkthrough: 'crowns' takes the first letters of 'The untimely death of Richard'. Henry Tudor defeated Richard III at Bosworth in 1485 and became Henry VII.
explanation.definitionFit: Henry Tudor won the Battle of Bosworth Field in 1485 and founded the royal dynasty of that name.

clue.text: Lost rings I'm returning

indicators.note: returning means the whole run of letters reads backwards

parts.note: to ring someone is to dial them, so rings gives dials
taken as written, without the apostrophe

explanation.surface: Someone who has lost their rings and is going back to look.
explanation.walkthrough: 'returning' turns DIALSIM, the run DIALS plus IM, into the answer. 'Rings' looks like jewellery but means phones.
explanation.definitionFit: Something mislaid has been put somewhere and forgotten, so it is lost.

clue.text: Raw, put in oven, getting cooked

indicators.note: one piece put in another goes inside it

parts.note: raw skin or meat is red
an oast is a kiln, an oven for drying hops

explanation.surface: Raw food placed in the oven and coming out cooked.
explanation.walkthrough: An oast is the kiln for drying hops, familiar from Kent farmland; 'Raw' means red, as raw skin or meat is.
explanation.definitionFit: Roasting is a way of cooking by dry heat, so roasted food has been cooked.

clue.text: Tower, first of places essayist's imprisoned

indicators.note: something imprisoned is held inside, so the essayist's name encloses a letter

parts.note: Richard Steele was an Irish-born essayist who founded The Tatler; the 's stands for 'has'

indicators.note: first of picks the opening letter of places

explanation.surface: A writer locked up in a tower, the first of several places.
explanation.walkthrough: 'imprisoned' puts P (first of 'places') inside STEELE. Richard Steele co-founded The Spectator with Joseph Addison.
explanation.definitionFit: A steeple is the tall tower of a church, usually topped by a spire.

clue.text: Press agency with power?

parts.note: press suggests the news media, but here it is pressing clothes, and the agency with power is a powered appliance

explanation.surface: An influential news agency.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Press agency' suggests a news service like Reuters, but here to press is to smooth clothes, and the agent doing it runs on mains power.
explanation.definitionFit: A household appliance heated by mains current, used to press creases out of fabric.
